title: Button
description: Turn an LED on while a pushbutton is pressed.

steps.clip: Grab an Arduino Uno and its USB cable, a breadboard, pushbutton, 10 kΩ resistor, 220 Ω resistor, LED and a few jumper wires.
Push the button into the breadboard so it sits across the middle gap: two legs above the gap, two below.
hints: The two legs in the same column — one above the gap, one below — are always connected inside the button.
Pressing the button connects its left column to its right column.
steps.goal: Put the button across the middle gap.

steps.clip: A jumper wire from the top half of the button's left column to pin 2 on the Arduino.
hints: Pin 2 is on the Arduino's row of numbered sockets.
Any free hole in that column works.
steps.goal: Connect one side of the button to pin 2.

steps.clip: A jumper wire from the button's right column (bottom half) to the + (red) row along the bottom edge — and, since this is the first thing using it, one more wire from that + row to the 5V pin on the Arduino (now the whole row is 5V).
hints: When you press, 5V flows through the button to the pin.
steps.goal: Connect the other side of the button to 5V.

steps.clip: Now a 10 kΩ resistor: one leg in the button's left column (bottom half), the other leg in an empty column.
hints: This is a pull-down: it keeps the pin at 0 (LOW) while the button isn't pressed.
Without it the pin 'floats' and reads random values.
steps.goal: Put a 10 kΩ resistor on the button's pin side.

steps.clip: A jumper wire from the resistor's other column to the − (blue) row along the bottom edge — and, since this is the first thing using it, one more wire from that − row to a GND pin on the Arduino (now the whole row is GND).
hints: Now the pin reads LOW, and HIGH only while you press.
steps.goal: Connect the pull-down resistor to GND.

steps.clip: Push a 220 Ω resistor into the breadboard, its two legs in two different numbered columns (leave some space from the last part).
hints: A resistor works either way round.
It protects the LED: without it too much current flows and the LED burns out.
steps.goal: Put the resistor for the LED on the breadboard.

steps.clip: A jumper wire from one of the resistor's columns to pin 13 on the Arduino.
hints: Pin 13 is on the Arduino's row of numbered sockets.
Any free hole in that column works.

steps.clip: Now the LED: its long leg in the same column as the resistor's other leg, its short leg in an empty column right next to it.
hints: The long leg is + (the anode) — it must face the resistor or the LED stays dark.
Legs in the same column are already connected.
steps.goal: Connect the LED's long leg (+) to the resistor.

steps.clip: A jumper wire from the short leg's column to the − (blue) row.
hints: The − row is already joined to GND.
steps.goal: Connect the LED's short leg (−) to GND.

steps.clip: Copy the code into the Arduino IDE and click Upload. Press the button: the LED lights up. Let go: it turns off.
